newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Ajax fan dies in bloody battle by appointment.
newsitem.headline: Ajax fan dies in bloody battle by appointment.

text.p: Hundreds of armed Dutch soccer fans fought on Sunday in a pre-planned battle in which a gang leader died and dozens of followers were injured.

The rival gangs outwitted police by naming their battlefield at the last minute and spreading the word by mobile telephone. Ajax Amsterdam and Feyenoord Rotterdam supporters answered the call by streaming to waste ground along the A9 motorway near Amsterdam, ready for a showdown with knives, clubs and baseball bats.
"I'm still stiff with shock," an elderly woman living nearby told Dutch radio. "There were hundreds of people chasing after each other with clubs, stoning each other."

Kennemerland chief of police Bob Visser told a news conference the authorities had expected a fight ahead of Feyenoord's match against AZ Alkmaar in the northern Netherlands but could not get to the scene in time to prevent bloodshed.

"We tried everything in our power to keep the two gangs apart, but we would have needed airborne troops to get between them," he said. "There was a brief and violent clash. Afterwards only the wounded were left, one of whom has since died."
He said an unknown number were still being treated for stab wounds at Beverwijk hospital.
Police had tried to prevent Feyenoord supporters from heading north to Amsterdam by closing off the Velser tunnel on the main highway. The fans used mobile phones to send their comrades another way.
Wil van Rhee, security manager for Dutch soccer association KNVB, said the dead man, a 35-year-old Amsterdammer, was a known Ajax ringleader.
"The fatality was one of the leaders of the Ajax gang, the heavily wounded man came from a similar group attached to Feyenoord," Van Rhee told Dutch news agency ANP.
Reuters photographer Jasper Juinen found the area littered with burned cars. Dutch riot police were scouring the wasteland for weapons. "The atmosphere is still very tense," he reported.

News that an Ajax supporter had been killed in fighting did not spoil the jubilant mood of Rotterdam fans at the Alkmaar ground after their teams's 2-0 away win. "I told you we were the best," one screamed at television cameras .
Police searched rowdy young Feyenoord fans wearing the team's black colours and checked their clothing for signs of blood stains. Two men were arrested after they were found carrying knives.
Hatred between Feyenoord and Amsterdam reflects the cultural divide between the Netherlands' two biggest cities.
Rough diamond Rotterdam has long felt looked down on by aristocratic Amsterdam. Rotterdammers say they make the Netherlands' money and Amsterdam spends it.

The teams' supporters are routinely separated at the stadiums and ugly confrontations which took place in the 1970s and 1980s had largely disappeared at matches themselves, replaced by tasteless chanting.
Sunday's clash appears to signal a new trend with so-called supporters arranging a battle rendezvous en route to games with other clubs.
Police defused a similar incident earlier this year, when they intervened in another pre-arranged war between Feyenoord and Ajax supporters in north Amsterdam.
Intelligence officers intercepted information about the planned clash and riot police were able to confiscate an arsenal of knives, baseball bats and iron bars, chains and pickaxes.
But on Sunday police were helpless to intervene.
Feyenoord chairman Jorien van Herik called it "a black day for Dutch football."
"It's really beyond our power," he told Dutch television. "This has nothing to do with football."
Ajax chairman Michael van Praag said that in the past he had called on other clubs and police to hammer out a joint policy to combat football violence. "Until now nothing has been done," he said.
Government ministers condemned the gangs and called for a new police clampdown on football violence.
Home affairs minister Hans Dijkstal said the government looked to be losing its grip on soccer hooliganism and urgently needed to review its strategy.
"This is hard work for the police," he said. "We must track down and punish these criminal gangs."

Along with their English counterparts, Dutch fans were among some of Europe's most feared soccer vandals in the 1970s, but improved policing methods based on tracking known hooligans brought violence under control.

In recent years, however, organised violence has become more difficult to trace, as fans no longer travel en masse to matches but make last-minute arrangements by mobile phone, a police intelligence officer warned in a recent newspaper interview.
